The Washington Post, by contrast, trains its attention on the human and economic toll of ending Temporary Protected Status for Haitians in Springfield, Ohio: reporting by Arelis R. Hernández and a companion piece describe a community driven into hiding, a workforce collapse the paper calls without precedent in scale, and a suicide linked to an ICE ankle monitor, explicitly suggesting a correlation between the deportation campaign and the city's economic damage.

4794.topic_label: Swiss air defense policy and international cooperation
4794.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column for Neue Zürcher Zeitung, Selina Berner argues that the long-standing Swiss belief in a self-sufficient national air defense - plausible during the Cold War - has become a dangerous illusion today. She contends that Switzerland can no longer defend its own airspace alone, and that political indecision together with chronic underfunding of domestic defense capacity leave the country dangerously exposed. Berner calls for closer international cooperation with the EU, NATO and the United States alongside greater investment in Switzerland's own defense industry, framing this as an urgent necessity rather than a mere policy option.

4795.topic_label: Release of Swiss/Austrian hostages held in Libya/Niger
4795.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by Neue Zürcher Zeitung, in a report bylined by Katharina Bracher. Rather than presenting the release of the Swiss and Austrian hostages after eighteen months in captivity in Niger as a straightforward humanitarian story, the article situates it within a wider geopolitical frame: observers are cited describing the release as a "diplomatic victory" for Libyan military strongman Khalifa Haftar, and the event is linked to a broader contest for influence in the Sahel involving the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Turkey. With no other source covering this story, there is no competing emphasis to contrast it with - the article's distinctive angle is simply its insistence on reading an apparently humanitarian resolution as a move in a regional power game.

4796.topic_label: Tensions in South China Sea and Taiwan Strait
4796.comparison_text: This topic is covered solely by Neue Zürcher Zeitung, in an article by Patrick Zoll. The piece frames the escalation through a sequence of incidents - a US warship's passage near Sabina Shoal, aggressive Chinese coast guard actions against the Philippines, and China's growing permanent presence near Taiwan's Pratas Island - and leans heavily on American voices, quoting a US official who describes Beijing's constant coast guard patrols as a form of warfare that is "extremely destabilizing." With no other source treating this topic, the report stands as a single, largely Washington-aligned perspective on China's regional assertiveness rather than part of a comparative debate.

4797.topic_label: CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins' standoff with Trump
4797.comparison_text: This topic is covered by only one source. In her column in Neue Zürcher Zeitung, Birgit Schmid profiles CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins as an unflappable journalist who withstands Trump's repeated insults and sexist jabs while continuing to press him with tough questions. Schmid argues that Trump's efforts to punish critical outlets have, paradoxically, only raised the profile of reporters like Collins rather than diminishing them.

4798.topic_label: Debate over Swiss financial sector's climate footprint
4798.comparison_text: In a column in Neue Zürcher Zeitung, David von Plon and Sebastian Briellmann argue that left-wing parties and environmental groups have distorted the findings of a McKinsey study by claiming it shows Swiss banks directly cause emissions 14 to 18 times Switzerland's domestic total, when the study in fact refers only to indirect "financed emissions" that banks neither generate nor control outright. The authors warn that unilateral, stricter Swiss regulation could backfire by pushing financial business abroad without any real reduction in global emissions. As this is the only source covering the topic, there is no cross-source contrast to draw here, only this single critical framing of how the study has been politically used.

4799.topic_label: Role of the state in economy and innovation (Mazzucato)
4799.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source: an interview in Neue Zürcher Zeitung with economist Mariana Mazzucato, titled "Hört auf, einfach Geld zu verschenken" ("Stop simply giving money away"). In it, Mazzucato argues that governments should abandon the role of passive grant-givers and instead act as active, intelligent drivers of innovation - setting conditions on support and sharing in the returns when they fund private companies. She is sharply critical of the accumulated market power of Big Tech and describes most public-private partnerships as "parasitic rather than symbiotic," lacking genuine reciprocity. Since no other outlet addresses this theme, there is no cross-source contrast to draw; the piece stands as Mazzucato's own argument, presented through an interview format in Neue Zürcher Zeitung rather than as the newspaper's institutional position.

4800.topic_label: India protests over Modi's voter list purges
4800.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by Neue Zürcher Zeitung. In his column there, Ulrich von Schwerin argues that Modi's heavy-handed crackdown on protesters against a flawed and opaque purge of voter lists - one that disproportionately hit Muslims and the poor - is disproportionate and politically motivated, warning that it is eroding trust in India's democratic process. With no other outlet weighing in, there is no cross-source contrast to draw on how the episode is being framed.

4801.topic_label: Feminism and the legacy of Emma magazine
4801.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column in Süddeutsche Zeitung, Johanna Pfund marks the end of Emma magazine's print edition as an occasion to reflect on the legacy of German feminism's pioneers, above all Alice Schwarzer, writing that "without them, women today would not be where they are." Yet Pfund insists the feminist project remains unfinished, and criticizes the tendency of rival feminist factions to reject one another, arguing that such infighting undermines causes that are otherwise legitimate. Since no other outlet addresses this topic, there is no cross-source contrast to draw - only Pfund's personal, signed perspective, which blends historical appreciation with an internal critique of the movement itself.

4802.comparison_text: As only one source addresses this topic, there is no cross-source contrast to draw out. In her column in Süddeutsche Zeitung, Lea Hampel argues that the multi-billion-euro savings CDU/CSU promised from tightening basic income support have failed to materialize, and that the reform has instead deepened social division without delivering any efficiency gains. She points to the blunt fact that, so far, nothing has been saved, as emblematic of the policy's failure.

4803.topic_label: Major powers blocking UN climate panel (IPCC) decisions
4803.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In his article in Süddeutsche Zeitung, Thomas Hummel reports that powerful states - Russia, Saudi Arabia, China and India - blocked key IPCC decisions on the timing and budget of the panel's next report, while the German government is pushing to keep the 2028 publication schedule intact. He cites experts who warn that delaying crucial climate science amounts to a "betrayal" of vulnerable developing countries that urgently need timely, science-based guidance for climate action. With no other outlet addressing the story, there is no competing framing to compare, but Hummel's piece itself casts the episode as a clash between the geopolitical interests of major powers and the pressing needs of vulnerable nations and climate science.

4804.topic_label: Volkswagen's struggles in the Chinese EV market
4804.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by Süddeutsche Zeitung, in an article signed by Christina Kunkel and Gregor Scheuner. The piece examines Volkswagen's "In China, for China" strategy, noting that despite developing new models with Chinese partners, sales have badly missed targets - averaging just 267 units a month between April and August against a planned 3,622. The authors stop short of calling the strategy a failure outright, pointing to bright spots such as hybrid models and Audi's submarket as reasons it may still be too early to render a final verdict.

4805.topic_label: Berlin housing/welfare policy and its democratic roots
4805.comparison_text: The two sources take opposite angles on Berlin's housing debate. In his column in Süddeutsche Zeitung, Heribert Prantl argues that the welfare provisions in the Berlin coalition's housing proposal echo a deep democratic tradition rooted in Bavaria's and Hesse's 1946 constitutions, and urges the CDU and CSU to reclaim rather than attack these social roots, warning that abandoning them cedes ground to the AfD's anti-welfare, radical-capitalist politics. The Washington Post, by contrast, in an unsigned editorial reflecting the paper's institutional position, attacks the Die Linke-backed proposal to nationalize large landlords' apartments as a doomed, market-distorting scheme, praising Chancellor Friedrich Merz for defending property rights and market-based solutions instead. Where Prantl frames social welfare policy as a legitimate continuation of German democratic tradition that conservatives should embrace, the Washington Post casts the same policy direction as a threat to property rights and free-market principles.

4806.topic_label: German support for Ukraine framed as national self-interest
4806.comparison_text: All three pieces on this topic come from Süddeutsche Zeitung, each adding a distinct layer to the argument. In his column, Ronen Steinke contends that mainstream German politicians back aid to Ukraine not out of pure charity but out of plain national self-interest - stopping Russian aggression before it reaches the EU - and criticizes them for refusing to say so openly, a silence he says lets populists falsely frame the issue as charity versus domestic needs. In a separate column, Peter Burghardt shifts the focus to Washington, condemning Trump and his envoy Witkoff for siding with Putin against Ukraine, calling it a tragedy, and urging members of Congress to speak out more forcefully. A third, unsigned report by Georg Ismar and Hubert Wetzel moves from commentary to reporting, revealing that the United States has halted deliveries of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, leaving it unable to intercept ballistic missiles, and citing experts who warn that this dependence on US supply is dangerous and that the delay may be a deliberate pressure tactic against Kyiv. Together, the three pieces build a picture in which the newspaper urges Germany to admit its self-interest openly while simultaneously warning that American conduct is undermining the very support Ukraine depends on.

4807.topic_label: Venezuela's political crisis after Maduro's capture
4807.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by USA Today, which reports on the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years in Venezuela, where thousands took to the streets demanding free elections following the US capture of Maduro and ongoing US-backed negotiations over the country's electoral future. The article highlights the notably light presence of security forces as evidence of a shifting political climate, and includes a protester's quote expressing hope that change is finally possible. As the only source covering this story, there is no competing framing to compare - the piece's emphasis rests entirely on cautious public optimism and the sense that genuine democratic change may be within reach.

4808.topic_label: Conviction of Kenyan doomsday cult leader for mass murder
4808.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a report bylined by Rael Ombuor, The Washington Post documents the conviction of Paul Nthenge Mackenzie and 28 associates for the deaths of 191 people, mostly children, in a doomsday cult in Kenya's Shakahola Forest. Beyond recounting the verdict, the piece places heavy emphasis on the failure of Kenyan authorities to intervene despite the scale of the deaths, quoting criticism that government laxity allowed the mass deaths to go unnoticed and calling for officials to be held accountable alongside the cult leader himself.

4809.topic_label: US deep-sea mining plans in the Pacific
4809.comparison_text: This topic is covered solely by USA Today, through two complementary articles that together present a single, largely critical angle. In her byline piece, Karissa Waddick reports on the Trump administration's plan to auction nearly 100 million acres of Pacific Ocean seafloor for mineral extraction, framing the move as a national-security measure meant to reduce US reliance on China, while giving substantial space to warnings from Pacific islanders and environmentalists about irreversible ecological harm, as well as to economists who question the venture's economic logic. The second, unsigned USA Today article narrows the focus specifically to American Samoa, detailing how local communities, indigenous groups and officials oppose the proposed leases and have filed a lawsuit to block them, citing fears of lasting damage to the ocean and to the territory's vital tuna industry. Together, the two pieces move from a broad strategic-versus-environmental framing to a close-up portrait of grassroots and legal resistance against federal policy.

4810.topic_label: Arab American political attitudes shift amid Gaza/Iran wars
4810.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. The Washington Post, in a report by Laura Beveridge and Scott Clement, presents findings from a Washington Post-Schar School poll showing a sharp swing among Arab American voters toward the Democratic Party, driven by deep disapproval of the Trump administration's handling of the Gaza and Iran wars and a widespread perception that the Republican Party is unfriendly toward Arab Americans. The piece highlights that nearly eight in ten respondents want reduced U.S. military support for Israel, with six in ten favoring ending it entirely, and that many respondents believe Israel has committed war crimes in Gaza. With no other outlet covering this story, there is no cross-source contrast to draw out.

4811.comparison_text: Both papers cover the same major PHP security flaw, but with different emphases. The Guardian, in a piece by Robert Booth and Aisha Down, centres the story on Britain - 32 UK government websites taken offline as a precaution - and adds a distinct intelligence-geopolitical angle, largely through former GCHQ chief David Omand's warning that Russia and China could exploit the bug. USA Today instead takes a broader global approach, tracking the exponential pace of exploitation attempts - from tens of thousands within 45 minutes to millions within two hours - and detailing the precautionary shutdowns by governments and companies across Japan, China, South Korea, Finland and France. Where The Guardian frames the episode primarily as a national security threat tied to geopolitical rivals, USA Today presents it mainly as a fast-moving global technological crisis.

4812.topic_label: Criticism of Cameroon's president residing abroad
4812.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by The Washington Post, in a report by Rael Ombuor, so there is no cross-source contrast to draw. The piece documents public criticism of Cameroon's 93-year-old president, Paul Biya, for repeatedly spending long stretches abroad in Switzerland even as the country grapples with high unemployment and an ongoing separatist conflict, and despite there being no vice president to fill the void. The report quotes ordinary Cameroonians voicing frustration at their head of state's prolonged absence, framing it as emblematic of a deeper governance crisis.

4813.topic_label: Calls for clearer US tariff legislation
4813.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column in The Washington Post, Matthew Lynn argues that the Trump administration's reliance on various obscure legal justifications to impose tariffs has produced a chaotic and legally dubious mess, and calls on Congress to establish a clear legal framework granting the president tariff authority within defined limits subject to oversight. With no other outlets addressing this topic, no cross-source comparison is possible.

4814.comparison_text: This topic is covered solely by The Washington Post, which reports on nationwide protests across Poland demanding liberalized abortion law. The article centers on activists' skeptical view that the Tusk government's draft legislation amounts to mere "token gestures" with no real chance of passage, since the conservative president is expected to veto any such bills, and notes that the timing - a year before the next parliamentary election - feeds suspicion that the move is more political theater than genuine reform. With no other source covering the story, there is no competing framing or emphasis to compare it against.

4815.topic_label: Pentagon pressure on US universities over China ties
4815.comparison_text: This topic is covered solely by The Washington Post, in an investigative piece by Todd Wallack. The article pushes back against the Pentagon's claim of victory - that all 30 universities ordered to cut China-linked ties had done so or mitigated the risk - by citing internal documents in which most of the schools insisted their partnerships never posed any genuine security threat, as captured in the quote that they met "none of the criteria in the letter or the press release that would be cause for concern." Wallack's framing thus casts doubt on the government's rationale, suggesting the crackdown's declared success overstates an actual threat that many institutions dispute ever existed.

4816.topic_label: Proposed US-China AI reporting/arms control framework
4816.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic comes from a single source. In a column in The Washington Post, Rohan Sharma argues that any bilateral US-China pact to govern dangerous AI capabilities must rest on reliable domestic reporting arrangements within the United States itself. He calls for negotiators to secure reciprocal commitments from both sides, and for Congress to pass clear statutory duties requiring designated US developers to report defined dangerous capabilities and serious security breaches within specified deadlines, via secure channels. As the only article on this topic, there is no cross-source contrast to draw - the piece stands as a single advocacy position for building robust legal infrastructure at home before or alongside any international arms-control agreement.

4817.topic_label: Alberta's separatism referendum and its aftermath
4817.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic comes exclusively from the Globe and Mail, in two signed columns by Tony Keller that share a single, consistent angle rather than offering competing perspectives. In his first column, Keller focuses on the economic payoff of separatism's crushing defeat, arguing that the landslide vote against separation - with roughly three-quarters of Albertans rejecting even the idea of holding a referendum - removes the uncertainty that had been discouraging investment in the province, and proves that separatist rhetoric never had genuine public backing. In his second column, Keller broadens the lens from economics to political culture, casting the entire separatist episode as a pointless "detour" that wasted a year of Alberta's political life, and insisting that voters were never fooled by the movement's leaders - captured in his pointed line that "you can't show people an anchor and tell them it's a kite." Both pieces rest on the same underlying judgment that separatism was a fringe phenomenon without real support, but the first stresses the relief this brings to investors while the second emphasizes the opportunity it now gives a united Canada to refocus on economic growth.

4818.topic_label: Western dependence on US defence technology
4818.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In his column in The Globe and Mail, Doug Saunders argues that the United States has weaponized its control over allied militaries' technology - satellite links, missile defence systems, intelligence-sharing - using it as political leverage against Ukraine, and warns that Washington could just as easily turn that same leverage against any NATO member. He concludes that Europe and Canada must urgently build independent defence capacity, since even an asset like the F-35 fighter jet could overnight become a liability if a US president turns against its purchasers.

4819.topic_label: British Columbia's provincial debt and election
4819.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In his column in The Globe and Mail, Gary Mason warns that British Columbia's ballooning public debt and spending under the NDP government echo the fiscal mess the Liberals once had to clean up, and argues that neither of the province's leading parties is showing the fiscal discipline needed to avert deeper trouble. With no other newspaper addressing the issue, there is no competing framing to compare - only Mason's own critical stance toward both major parties.

4820.comparison_text: This topic is covered by only one source. In a column in the Globe and Mail, Hungary's ambassador Miklós Lengyel marks the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, arguing that its lessons about freedom, sovereignty and solidarity remain vital today. Lengyel emphasizes the Canada-Hungary bond in particular, crediting Canada's welcoming of Hungarian refugees after 1956 as a formative and enduring connection between the two countries, and insisting that freedom and democracy are not automatic gifts but must be fought for continually. As this is a single-source piece, there is no cross-source contrast to draw - only the ambassador's own commemorative and diplomatic framing.

4821.topic_label: Canada denies US accusations of midterm election interference
4821.comparison_text: Both articles on this topic come from the Globe and Mail, which effectively tells this story in two stages rather than offering competing angles. The first, bylined by Stephanie Levitz and Sean Silcoff, centres on Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's flat denial of US embassy accusations that Canada is meddling in the midterms, framing the episode around internal guidance urging Canadian diplomats to limit public appearances alongside American politicians - emphasizing the broader diplomatic friction tied to the tariff dispute. The second, unsigned, article widens the lens to include Ontario Premier Doug Ford's declaration that he has "no interest" in influencing the US vote, and quotes at length the US warning that "all Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way." Where the first piece frames the story mainly as an official Canadian denial, the second foregrounds the sweeping nature of the American demand and draws in more Canadian political figures, underscoring how the election-interference accusations are becoming entangled with the wider US-Canada standoff.

4822.topic_label: Canada-US steel trade dispute and Stelco layoffs
4822.comparison_text: All four pieces on this topic come from the Globe and Mail, yet they approach the same dispute from distinct angles. In his column, Jason Kirby challenges the very premise of the crisis, arguing that Cleveland-Cliffs' CEO's claim of an "avalanche" of foreign steel dumping into Canada is contradicted by trade data showing galvanized steel imports down 30 to 60 percent. By contrast, Niall McGee's news report focuses on the regulatory and political fallout, detailing how Canada's Industry Minister is threatening legal action against Cleveland-Cliffs/Stelco for breaching employment commitments under the Investment Canada Act, amid the company's vocal support for Trump's tariff policies. Mark Rendell's news report widens the lens to the broader bilateral trade negotiations, quoting Canada's chief negotiator as saying there is no timeline for resuming formal talks and that a return to pre-Trump free trade is unlikely. In her column, Rita Trichur draws a policy conclusion from the same turmoil, arguing that the severity of the crisis justifies bolder government intervention - including equity stakes in companies - as long as it stops short of protectionism. Together, the two news reports chart the institutional standoff between Ottawa, Washington and the company, while the two columns offer competing interpretations - one debunking the import-surge narrative, the other urging more assertive state action.

4823.topic_label: US courts forcing accountability on Big Tech
4823.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic comes from a single source. In her column in The Globe and Mail, Cecilia Kang argues that with Congress largely stalled, it is the courts that have become the real engine of accountability for Big Tech, pointing to record penalties and lawsuits against companies like Meta and Google over addictive product design and data privacy practices. Her framing casts litigation, rather than legislation, as the decisive force reshaping how tech giants operate, positioning the judiciary as the institution actually delivering regulatory consequences that lawmakers have failed to produce.

4824.topic_label: Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi contacts her son after years
4824.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic comes from a single source. The Guardian reports that Aung San Suu Kyi's son, Kim Aris, was able to speak with her by phone for the first time in more than five years, quoting his statement that "today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years." The article frames the development both as a result of sustained international pressure for proof of life regarding the detained leader and as part of the military junta's broader effort to project an image of legitimacy by easing some restrictions on her.

4825.topic_label: Canada's Supreme Court appeal over 2022 Emergencies Act use
4825.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic comes solely from The Globe and Mail, in a report by David Ebner. The article focuses on the legal trajectory of the case, noting that Ottawa lost twice in lower courts, which found the government had not shown reasonable grounds for declaring a national emergency or that the 2022 trucker protests could not have been resolved through existing laws. It lays out both the federal government's arguments and those of civil liberties groups, and notes questions raised about judicial bias, presenting the dispute in largely factual, legal-analytical terms rather than advocating a position.

4826.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): The author warns that right-wing populists like Weidel and Le Pen want to dismantle Brussels institutions, but argues the EU needs strong, unified institutions now more than ever to avoid being crushed between right and left populism and in the competition with Russia, China and the US. Key excerpt: "Die EU droht zerrieben zu werden zwischen dem Populismus von rechts und links."

4827.topic_label: Economic policy and right-wing populism / anti-fascist economics debate
4827.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): The author reviews economist Isabella Weber's book arguing that unaffordable prices and material insecurity drive voters toward far-right parties, citing Mamdani's NYC policies and the Weimar-era precedent, but is skeptical that affordability alone would curb parties like the AfD or Trump's movement. Key excerpt: "Weber empfiehlt die gerechtere Verteilung von Wohlstand als Mittel gegen Rechtsradikalismus."

4828.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): The author argues Putin's war against Ukraine is an attack on all of Europe, exploiting AfD and BSW to spread fear and erode German support for Ukraine; abandoning Ukraine would be both a political folly and a moral failure. Key excerpt: "Putins Angriff auf die Ukraine ist ein Angriff auf Europa, in verschiedenen Formen und mit verschiedenen Intensitäten geführt."

4829.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Reports that Zelenskyy's relations with Washington have deteriorated after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived sanctions on Moscow, while urging Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, as Russia and Ukraine continued mutual missile and drone strikes. Key excerpt: "Zelenskyy’s relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow."

4830.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Investigative report revealing that a major new donor to Nigel Farage's Reform UK party had past business dealings with an Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country's supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with Iran. Key excerpt: "a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari's past dealings with Iranian"

4831.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): EU officials say the UK, Canada and Japan should contribute more financially to Ukraine's defence, as Ukraine faces a €70bn funding shortfall in 2027 and the US appears to be shifting its stance. Key excerpt: "We urgently need other partners to step up."

4832.topic_label: Nigel Farage's Reform UK donor's business ties to Iranian state-linked foundation
4832.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Investigative report detailing how Reform UK donor Sasan Ghandehari was the major investor in a telecoms joint venture with AQR, a bonyad religious foundation controlled by Iran's supreme leader apparatus, raising questions about sanctions, hardliners, and the sourcing of his fortune. Key excerpt: "The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail."

4833.topic_label: Western fascination with China's system vs. US decline
4833.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Neubacher criticizes the trend of Westerners romanticizing Chinese lifestyle and authoritarian efficiency on social media while ignoring surveillance, censorship, and repression; he worries the West may be losing the systemic competition against authoritarianism as the US under Trump self-destructs, though he hopes China's aging, state-capitalist system isn't attractive enough to win. Key excerpt: "Chinesische Kultur wirkt umso interes santer, je mehr die USA unter Donald Trump kaputtgehen."

4834.topic_label: German fuel price cap debate amid oil/Iran-war-linked price crisis
4834.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): The article reports on internal German coalition disputes over a planned fuel price cap modeled on Luxembourg/Belgium, noting Economy Minister Reiche opposes it while SPD figures support it, and cites experts warning it could legally enshrine oil companies' excess profits rather than curb them, with the price surge linked to the Iran war's effect on refinery margins. Key excerpt: "Diese Differenz sei seit Ausbruch des Irankriegs Ende Februar in die Höhe geschnellt."
